verses.translation_literal: And Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, eunuch of Pharaoh, chief of the bodyguards, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.
verses.translation_dramatic: Down to Egypt they had carried Joseph, down from the hills and into the black river-land. And there an Egyptian named Potiphar, Pharaoh's own officer, captain of the royal guard, bought him from the hands of the Ishmaelites who had brought him.
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator picks up the thread dropped at 37:36, after the Judah and Tamar interlude, and says twice, in two forms of one verb, that Joseph was taken down (hurad ... horiduhu). For Joseph every stage of the journey is a descent. The KJV's "officer" for saris hides a fact: the word is the ordinary term for a court official and also the word for a eunuch, and the ancient readers noticed, because this man has a wife. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan says outright that Potiphar was made a eunuch as punishment for buying Joseph with ill intent. The KJV's "captain of the guard" for sar hatabbachim smooths over a harder edge: the words mean chief of the slaughterers (or cooks), and Rashbam explains that the condemned and the prisoners were judged through him, which is why Joseph will end up in this man's own prison. The KJV's "bought him of the hands" uses old "of" for "from": the money passed from hand to hand, and a person became property.

philological_notes.note: Court official; the same word is used for eunuchs, and its range is debated. The text calls Potiphar a saris and also gives him a wife, so 'official' is the safe sense and 'eunuch' the older etymological one. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan takes it as castration.
Literally 'chief of the slaughterers/cooks'; as an office, the commander of the royal bodyguard, who also kept the prison and saw to sentences.
'Was brought down'; the verb returns in horiduhu at the end of the verse and echoes Judah's going down in 38:1. Rashi says the chapter is placed here to join Joseph's descent with Judah's.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH was with Joseph, and he was a man succeeding, and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD was with Joseph. Whatever his hands took up came to good, and he lived on, a man whose work succeeded, in the house of his Egyptian master.
verses.directors_commentary: Notice who is named first. Joseph is a slave, bought and sold, yet the sentence begins with the LORD. "Was with" is the Genesis formula for God's covenant presence, the thing foreign rulers say about Abraham (21:22) and Isaac (26:28); it is not a vague blessing. The KJV's "prosperous man" is acceptable but flattens a wordplay that the next verse completes: here Joseph is the matslich, the one who succeeds, and in verse 3 YHWH is the one who matslich, makes succeed, in his hand. Same word; the narrator will not let you separate Joseph's competence from God's gift. Mark the divine name too: Genesis 37 and 40 to 50 speak of God as Elohim, but the narrator of this chapter uses YHWH, while Joseph, speaking to Egyptians, will say Elohim (v. 9). "His master" is plural in form (adonav), a plural of rank, which the KJV's singular rightly reflects. Radak reads the success as total, in every errand his master sent him on.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle: 'one who succeeds / brings to a good end'. Verse 3 uses the same form of YHWH ('making succeed'), so the English should echo it.
'YHWH was with Joseph' with the preposition et; the covenant-presence formula, as in 26:28. Sforno reads it as protection from those who rose against him.

verses.translation_literal: And his master saw that YHWH was with him, and all that he was doing, YHWH was making succeed in his hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: His master saw it. Some things cannot be hidden: the LORD was with this man, and whatever he turned his hand to, the LORD made it come right in that hand.
verses.directors_commentary: What exactly does an Egyptian see? Rashi says that the name of heaven was always on Joseph's lips, so the master heard the God of Joseph from Joseph himself. Ramban doubts that and argues that Potiphar saw results beyond what any man's work explains, and drew the conclusion as Abimelech did of Isaac (26:28, "we saw plainly that the LORD was with you"). The text only says he saw it. In a world where good fortune is the gods' business, a slave whose every task thrives is a living omen. The KJV is close, but notice "hand": it is the thread of this section, and everything is put in Joseph's hand: his work (v. 3), the household (v. 4), the master's goods (vv. 6, 8), and at the end a garment (v. 12). Keep "hand" wherever the English can carry it.

philological_notes.note: 'In his hand': the instrument of work and of trust. The chapter keeps returning to the hand (vv. 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), so the English should keep 'hand' where it can.
Ramban holds that the master perceived God's help from visible results; Rashi says Joseph spoke God's name constantly.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph found favor in his eyes, and served him, and he appointed him over his house, and all that there was to him he gave into his hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph found favor in his master's eyes, and so he was set to wait upon him in person; then the master put him in charge of the whole house, and everything he owned he gave into Joseph's hand.
verses.directors_commentary: Three steps of promotion are packed into one verse. First "found favor in his eyes" (chen), the courtier's phrase for a patron's pleasure. Then vayesharet, "served him", not the verb of a field slave but the one for a personal attendant; Radak and Sforno take it as waiting upon his master's own person and needs. Then vayafkidehu, "appointed him over his house", the office of steward: he holds the stores, the staff and the accounts. The KJV's "made him overseer" is adequate, though it uses a noun where the Hebrew has a verb, "appointed". The rabbis, as Ramban reports from Genesis Rabbah, imagined Potiphar suspecting sorcery from so much success until he saw the divine presence standing over Joseph. The Hebrew itself says only that favor came first and authority after.

philological_notes.note: 'Served': personal service to a person of rank, as a courtier attends, not a labourer's work.
Hiphil 'he appointed/put in charge'; the steward's office. The root returns in v. 5.
'All that there is to him'; Rashi notes the clipped syntax, with 'asher' (that) omitted.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, from then he had appointed him in his house and over all that there was to him, that YHWH blessed the house of the Egyptian on account of Joseph; and the blessing of YHWH was on all that there was to him, in the house and in the field.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the day Joseph was set over the house and over all that was his, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's household for Joseph's sake. The blessing of the LORD lay upon everything the man owned, within the walls and out in the field.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the narrator states the theology outright: the blessing comes "on account of Joseph" (biglal Yosef), and the one who benefits is a foreigner. It reads like the promise to Abraham at work (12:3), though the text does not say so. The Hebrew repeats the root brk, "blessed ... the blessing of", and the English should repeat it too. Another KJV habit: it renders hifqid as "made him overseer", which supplies a noun the Hebrew lacks; the text says only "appointed" (the root pqd). "In the house and in the field" names the two halves of an estate: the household and its stores on one side, grain and herds on the other. Nothing here suggests the Egyptian asked for the blessing or prayed for it; it came to him by proximity to Joseph.

philological_notes.note: 'On account of, for the sake of'; a causal preposition that makes Joseph the reason for the household's blessing.
'Appointed, put in charge'. KJV 'made overseer' adds a noun the Hebrew lacks.

verses.translation_literal: And he left all that was his in the hand of Joseph, and he did not know with him anything except the bread which he was eating. And Joseph was beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance.
verses.translation_dramatic: He left everything he had in Joseph's hand, and kept no reckoning of anything but the bread he ate. And Joseph was fair of form and fair to look upon.
verses.directors_commentary: Two sentences, one door closing and one opening. First: Potiphar "knew nothing with him" except "the bread". The KJV's "he knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat" keeps the riddle, and the riddle is old. Rashi, following Genesis Rabbah as Ramban reports, says "bread" is a clean word for his wife. Ibn Ezra rejects that, partly because the master was a eunuch, and suggests instead that Potiphar left his food alone because Egyptians could not eat with Hebrews (43:32). Ramban and Radak allow either. Keep "bread" in English and let the audience feel both. Second: Joseph is "beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance", the same pair of phrases the text used of his mother Rachel (29:17), as Ibn Ezra notes. Here the beauty is not praise; it is the spark that sets off verse 7. The KJV's "goodly person, and well favoured" turns two matching phrases into two different ones.

philological_notes.note: 'The bread' = food, as 'lechem' can stand for any meal. Rashi reads it as a euphemism for Potiphar's wife; Ibn Ezra as food an Egyptian would not share with a Hebrew.
'Beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance'; the same pair is used of Rachel in 29:17, as Ibn Ezra notes: 'like his mother'.

verses.translation_literal: And it was after these things, and the wife of his master lifted up her eyes to Joseph, and she said: Lie with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: After this, the wife of his master lifted her eyes to Joseph, and looked, and kept looking. Then she said it plainly, two words: "Lie with me."
verses.directors_commentary: "Lifted up her eyes" is the Hebrew idiom for a deliberate look, one that decides something (Abraham looks up and sees the ram, Lot looks up at the Jordan plain). The KJV's "cast her eyes upon" is a little softer, as if her eyes had wandered; the Hebrew says she raised them, on purpose. The BBE's "looking on Joseph with desire ... be my lover" turns the sentence into romance. What the woman actually says is shikhvah immi: an imperative, two words, no name, no endearment, no condition. She speaks as the owner's wife to a slave. Her own name is never given; the text calls her only "the wife of his master", a title that makes the request an act against the master's house. A similar story in the Egyptian Tale of Two Brothers, where a brother's wife propositions the young hero, is rebuffed, and accuses him falsely, is often compared, though the Bible's version stands on its own. Radak says the episode is written so that readers may learn Joseph's self-mastery.

philological_notes.note: Idiom 'lifted up her eyes': a deliberate, appraising look; KJV 'cast her eyes' loses the sense of purpose.
Bare imperative 'Lie with me!', with the blunt verb for sexual intercourse. No courtesy form; the BBE's 'be my lover' softens it.
'After these things': a narrator's hinge. Radak connects this trial to Joseph's rise: it came after he was safe and prosperous.

verses.translation_literal: And he refused, and said to the wife of his master: Look, my lord does not know with me what is in the house, and all that there is to him he has given into my hand.
verses.translation_dramatic: He refused. He would not. And he said to the wife of his master, "Look. My lord does not ask me what is in the house; everything that is his he has put into my hand."
verses.directors_commentary: Vayma'en is the strong, piel form of "refuse": a flat, immovable no. The same verb describes Jacob when he refused to be comforted for Joseph (37:35); the family that refused comfort now produces the son who refuses seduction. The KJV's "But he refused" is accurate. Joseph's speech is built from the narrator's own words: "knows nothing with me" (v. 6), "gave into my hand" (v. 4). He answers with the facts of his master's trust, and by calling Potiphar adoni, "my lord", he reminds her whose house this is. Ramban notes that the text says "to the wife of his master", spelling out who she is and who he is, a servant speaking to his lord's wife, and still he refuses because he feared God more. The KJV's "wotteth" is a dead English word for "knows".

philological_notes.note: Piel of ma'en, 'to refuse', an emphatic, settled refusal; compare Jacob refusing comfort (37:35).
'Look! / See!' An attention particle, an appeal to the plain evidence.

verses.translation_literal: He is not greater in this house than I, and he has not withheld from me anything except you, in that you are his wife; and how shall I do this great evil, and sin to God?
verses.translation_dramatic: "No one in this house is greater than I. He has kept nothing back from me but you, because you are his wife. How could I do this great evil, and sin against God?"
verses.directors_commentary: Joseph's argument has two steps, and the order matters. First, human betrayal: Potiphar has put everything in his hand except one thing, and the exception is named, "you ... because you are his wife". Ramban says he begins with the betrayal of a trusting master because a woman may feel more weight in that than in the law of God. Second, divine: "sin against God" (Elohim). Joseph does not say YHWH to an Egyptian; he uses the word any nation understands, so the claim reaches beyond Israel. Rashi and Ramban say the sons of Noah were already commanded against sexual offenses. Compare Abimelech in 20:6, kept from "sinning" over Sarah. The KJV's "wickedness" for ra'ah is heavier than the plain word, which means evil, harm, calamity. Note too that the Hebrew has Joseph say that Potiphar himself is not greater in this house than he, which is as much as a slave can claim.

philological_notes.note: 'And I would sin to God.' The perfect with waw continues the question 'how shall I...'. Elohim, not YHWH, since Joseph speaks to an Egyptian. Rashi and Ramban: Noah's descendants were commanded to avoid illicit relations.
'The great evil'; ra'ah covers moral evil and harm both. KJV 'wickedness' is heavier than the word.
'Except you'; Sforno says the one thing withheld was the marriage relation alone.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, as she spoke to Joseph day, day, that he did not listen to her, to lie beside her, to be with her.
verses.translation_dramatic: Day after day she spoke to Joseph, and day after day he would not listen to her, not to lie beside her, not even to be with her.
verses.directors_commentary: The Hebrew has just two words for the length of the siege: yom yom, "day day". The KJV's "day by day" is acceptable, but the bare repetition is the sound of a drip on stone. "Did not listen to her" (shama el) means "did not obey", not that he did not hear: he heard all of it. The two infinitives, "to lie beside her, to be with her", are not alternatives, as the KJV's inserted "or" suggests; they are two rungs of a ladder. Ibn Ezra and Ramban take "beside her" as lying near without touching, and "to be with her" as even talking with her in private; Rashi hears the second as "to be with her in the world to come", a share in her punishment. Joseph refused the first rung as well as the last. Rashbam adds that he took care not even to be alone with her, until a day came when he had no choice.

philological_notes.note: 'To lie beside her'; Ibn Ezra and Ramban: even lying near her without intercourse, since 'etzel' is not used elsewhere of the act itself.
'To be with her'; Ibn Ezra: even to talk with her; Rashi, by Midrash: to share her fate in the world to come.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, on a day like this, that he came into the house to do his work, and there was no man of the men of the house there in the house.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then came a day like all the others, and Joseph went into the house to do his work. And there was no one inside, not one of the household men.
verses.directors_commentary: "On a day like this" (kehayom hazeh) is an idiom meaning "one such day"; the KJV's "about this time" turns a plot marker into a time stamp. Ibn Ezra asks how long after the first proposal it was: a week, a month, a year. The subject of "came" is not named in Hebrew, only "he"; the KJV supplies Joseph. "His work" (melakhto) is ambiguous: Onkelos and Ibn Ezra take it as the accounts and estate business, as steward; the Talmud (Sotah 36b), which Rashi cites, records a dispute over whether it meant his proper work or something else. The text itself blames no one here. The house is empty of "the men of the house", the male household staff, and the Hebrew names the house three times in one line (habaytah, anshei habayit, babayit), building a sense of an enclosed place. Rashi's midrash that it was a festival day when the household went to a temple has no support in the text; the narrator gives the emptiness, not the cause.

philological_notes.note: Idiom 'on a day like this', i.e. 'one day'. Ibn Ezra asks how long after the first proposal: a week, a month, or a year.
'His work/business'; Onkelos: checking accounts. Rashi cites Rav and Shmuel (Sotah 36b) on whether it was real work or something else.

verses.translation_literal: And she seized him by his garment, saying: Lie with me! And he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and went out, outside.
verses.translation_dramatic: She caught him by his garment. "Lie with me!" she said. And he left the garment in her hand, and fled, and went out into the open.
verses.directors_commentary: The same two words of verse 7, shikhvah immi, return, but now with a hand on him. And the verb that answers is a quiet echo: vaya'azov, "he left". In verse 6 Potiphar left (vaya'azov) everything in Joseph's hand; now Joseph leaves (vaya'azov) his garment in her hand. What Potiphar entrusted, Joseph keeps faith with; what she grabs, he lets go. The garment (beged) is the third piece of clothing in the story so far: the tunic dipped in blood (37:31-33) and Tamar's veil (chapter 38). Again clothing will be used to tell a lie. Ramban reasons that the bigd was a wrap that Joseph slipped off rather than break her grip, out of respect for his mistress, and that she then feared he would tell and spoke first. Sforno has Joseph running from the room, then walking calmly outside, so that no one would ask what he fled from. The KJV's "got him out" renders vayetze hachutzah, "he went out, outside"; the three verbs (left, fled, went out) come in rapid sequence.

philological_notes.note: 'His garment, outer wrap'; Ramban: a cloak he could wrap around himself. The word returns several more times in the chapter.
'And he left'. The same verb and form as in v. 6 ('he left all that he had in Joseph's hand'); keep one English word for both.
'And he fled'; Sforno: from the room, in case the evil impulse overcame him.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled outside,
verses.translation_dramatic: And then she saw it: the cloth hanging empty in her own fist, and the man gone, out through the door and into the light.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is a hinge: a single clause of pure observation, with no speech, while the woman's mind turns from desire to self-protection. Play the silence. The Hebrew says only 'when she saw'; what she decides is left for the next verse to show.

The KJV's 'fled forth' is faithful but archaic; the Hebrew is a plain, fast 'and he fled outside' (hachutzah), the same word that will be repeated in her story to make Joseph's flight sound like guilt. Watch how many times 'garment in hand' returns: it is the only physical evidence in the case, and every retelling will turn it.

philological_notes.note: 'His garment': the same root means 'to act treacherously' (bagad), so the word is one consonant-shift away from betrayal. The piece of cloth is both Joseph's innocence left behind and the 'proof' she will use. This is an observation about the root family, not a claim that the narrator is punning.

verses.translation_literal: And she called to the men of her house and said to them, saying: See, he has brought to us a man, a Hebrew, to laugh at us. He came to me to lie with me, and I called with a great voice.
verses.translation_dramatic: She did not wait for him to be gone. She called the household in, the men of the house, and she gave them the word before the cloth in her hand could say anything else. "Look at this," she said. "He has brought us a man, a Hebrew, and now he laughs at us." Her voice climbed. "He came to me, to lie with me. And I cried out. I cried out with a great voice."
verses.directors_commentary:
Watch whom she speaks to and how. She summons the men of her house, the slaves and staff, not her husband, and she does it as a woman whose status is her protection: in an Egyptian household the mistress's word, spoken loud and early, becomes the story everyone else repeats. She builds a coalition before the master returns. Her very first words turn the sin around. 'See, he has brought to us' blames the man who bought Joseph, her husband, without naming him; Rashi and Ibn Ezra both hear a jab at him, and Ramban hears a polite wife's way of not naming her lord. The KJV 'he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us' keeps the sense but turns Joseph into a category.

That category matters. The Hebrew is 'ish 'ivri, 'a man, a Hebrew': two nouns side by side, as if she cannot bring herself to say his name. Joseph is never named by her in this scene. 'Hebrew' is mostly a word on foreigners' lips, or used when speaking to foreigners; Ramban reads it here as playing on Egyptian contempt for Hebrews, citing Gen 43:32, where Egyptians could not eat bread with them. She is calling on the household's prejudice as much as on its loyalty. (The KJV and ASV 'an Hebrew' / 'a Hebrew' keep the label but lose the 'man' standing apart from it.)

Then 'to mock', lətsaheq. The KJV 'to mock us' is safe and flat. The root is the one in Isaac's name, 'laughter / play'; in other places it can mean sexual play, and here it hovers between 'to make a fool of us' and something rougher. It is the Hebrew word that sits closest to what she means but is unwilling to say. Notice the plural, 'us': she wants the household to feel injured, not just herself.

Last, the noise. 'I called with a great voice' is a claim the staff can test against what they heard. Radak notes that no one was in the house (39:11), so her cry is how they came; Rashbam says she raised her voice because they were far away, otherwise he would have lain with her by force. The hearers must believe she screamed before he fled, which is the lie's weakest point and its best prop.

philological_notes.note: 'Hebrew'. Rashi explains it as 'from across the river', after the ancestor Eber (Genesis Rabbah). In Genesis the word is mostly used by foreigners or when speaking to foreigners, as the wife does here; the Israelites more often call themselves by their own names. In her mouth it marks Joseph as an outsider to the house.

Literally 'to laugh at / play with us'. Same root as Isaac (Yitzhak) and as the 'playing' of Ishmael in Gen 21:9. The word keeps a possible sexual overtone, but the verse does not say it; that overtone is my reading. The 'us' is plural, inviting the household to share her grievance.

'He has brought to us': the subject is left unstated. Rashi and Ibn Ezra identify him as her husband; Radak glosses it 'how he has brought us this man'. It is her way of laying the blame on the master.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when he heard that I raised my voice and called out, that he left his garment beside me, and fled, and went out to the outside.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'And when he heard me lift my voice and cry out, he left his garment lying beside me, and he ran, and he was gone, out through the door.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Here she tells the truth about the garment and bends only what it means. In verses 12 and 13 the Hebrew has him leave the garment in her hand (beyadah); here it lies beside her (etzli), a word that cannot say who was holding what. The cloth that was torn from his body or slipped from his shoulders in the struggle now becomes something he dropped as he fled in panic at her cry. Radak, reading her speech as a claim, supplies what she implies: that she seized him by his clothes to hold him until the household arrived.

The verbs run as a chain of three: he left, he fled, he went out. Sforno notes that the household had seen him go outside, so to them she tells exactly what they saw. The KJV's 'got him out' is a little archaic, and the Hebrew is plainer: he went to the outside. The story depends on the cry causing the flight: 'when he heard that I raised my voice'. It is the same point as in verse 14, now as cause and effect, and she will repeat it to her husband in verse 18.

philological_notes.note: 'Beside me', 'by me'. A neutral word of nearness. In verses 12-13 the garment is in her hand (beyadah); the change from 'in her hand' to 'beside me' is her retelling.
'I raised my voice'. The Hiphil of rum, 'to be high', here with kol, 'voice', the idiom for crying out, as in the KJV's 'lifted up'. It echoes the 'great voice' of verse 14.

verses.translation_literal: And she laid down his garment beside her until his master came to his house.
verses.translation_dramatic: And she kept it. She laid his garment down beside her, and waited, until his master came home.
verses.directors_commentary:
A quiet, cold verse. The woman who just screamed now sits calmly with the cloth and waits for the right audience. The hinge is 'his master': the narrator calls Potiphar 'Joseph's master', not 'her husband' (Rashi: adoniv is Joseph's). From Joseph's side of the story this is a household slave and his owner; from hers, a marriage she is about to use.

The KJV's 'laid up' suggests she stored it away; the Hebrew verb (vatanach) is 'she set down, she left it', with the sense of a prop placed on stage. The garment is evidence and an alibi.

philological_notes.note: 'His master', plural of majesty with a singular sense, a regular form for an owner. Rashi: it refers to Joseph's master.

verses.translation_literal: And she spoke to him according to these words, saying: He came to me, the servant, the Hebrew, whom you brought to us, to mock in me.
verses.translation_dramatic: And to him she said the same words, the very same, and she said them with her eyes on his. 'He came to me, that servant, that Hebrew you brought among us. He came to make sport of me.'
verses.directors_commentary:
She tells her husband what she told the household, and the changes are small and sharp. In verse 14 Joseph was 'a man, a Hebrew'; now he is 'the servant, the Hebrew'. The word ish is gone and eved is in, so she names his slave status and says nothing of his office, though in this house he has been over everything (39:4-5). A slave who touches his master's wife is a different matter from a trusted steward. The KJV's 'Hebrew servant' puts the adjective first and loses the stress of the Hebrew word order, in which he is named only after the verb: 'he came to me, the servant, the Hebrew'.

The blame also moves. In verse 14 the unnamed bringer was left unspoken; here it is spoken, and to the bringer's face: 'whom you brought to us'. 'To mock us' has become 'to mock me': the audience is her husband, and she is the injured one. Radak says the phrase 'according to these words' means she said the same in substance, more or less, and the matter is one. Verses 17 and 18 are one speech: she keeps the cry (verse 18 is the cry again, nearly word for word with verse 15) and drops only 'to lie with me' (verse 14) and 'went out' (verse 15). Ramban, commenting on verse 19, notes the point behind this omission: a woman who had really been violated would hide it from her husband, so the midrash that she spoke in the language of intimacy is unlikely; what she says here is 'to mock', and the rest is left for him to hear.

philological_notes.note: 'The servant, the Hebrew': two definite nouns, as a contemptuous label. The first is the word for slave or servant; compare her 'a man' in verse 14.
'Whom you brought to us': the unnamed subject of verse 14 is now stated, and aimed at him.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when I lifted my voice and called out, that he left his garment beside me and fled outside.
verses.translation_dramatic: "But when I lifted my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me, and ran, out into the open."
verses.directors_commentary:
The last beat of her speech is shorter than in v. 15: 'went out' is gone, and only 'fled outside' remains. The editing is the point: a tidy sequence, scream, cloth, flight, with the cloth presented as the proof she holds up.

The KJV's 'fled out' is accurate but it blurs the rhythm: three beats of lifting, leaving, running. The literal layer keeps them.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, when his master heard [obj] the words of his wife which she spoke to him, saying: According to these things your servant did to me, that his nose burned.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when Joseph's master heard what his wife had said to him, "This is what your slave did to me," the anger rose in him and burned.
verses.directors_commentary:
The idiom is physical: 'his nose burned' (vayichar apo). Anger in Hebrew is heat in the nostrils, the flaring of a bull. The KJV's 'his wrath was kindled' is correct, but it loses that the body is on fire.

The stress falls on what is not said: Potiphar's anger is not narrated as being 'against Joseph'. Ibn Ezra notes that Potiphar did not kill him, 'because the matter was in doubt'; Sforno says the anger was at the household insult and that Potiphar believed Joseph more than her, but jailed him to satisfy her honor. For an Egyptian owner, a slave accused of touching his wife could have been put to death, so the prison is itself a mercy. The midrash that she said this in bed (Rashi on Genesis 39:19) is a minority reading that Ramban himself finds unlikely.

Notice 'your servant' (avdekha): she turns the possessive back on him.

philological_notes.note: 'His nose burned': Hebrew anger is heat in the nostrils (af means 'nose' and 'anger'). KJV 'wrath was kindled' keeps the fire but drops the body.

Ramban discusses two readings: 'in the very words I told the household', or the midrashic 'matters of intimacy' (Rashi). Ramban prefers the first and notes the kaf here is intensifying, citing Gen 24:28 and 44:7.

verses.translation_literal: And the master of Joseph took him and put him into the house of the Sohar, a place where the prisoners of the king [were] bound, and he was there in the house of the Sohar.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the master of Joseph rose, and took him, and gave him over. Not to the sword. To the house of the Sohar, the place where the king's own prisoners are bound. And there he was: there, in the house of the Sohar, among the bound.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this one quietly, because the text is surprisingly gentle with Potiphar. A slave accused of assaulting his master's wife could expect death (Ramban says as much on 39:19); Potiphar takes Joseph and puts him in a prison instead. Ibn Ezra says he did not kill him because the matter was in doubt for him; Sforno thinks he trusted Joseph's word more but jailed him to honor his wife; Radak says he believed her. The commentators split, and the verse does not say. The KJV 'Joseph's master' is right, but the Hebrew 'adone is the plural of majesty, 'masters of', used as a singular, as in 39:2 and 39:19.

The prison itself is named twice and each time by an unusual word, bet hassohar. The KJV and ASV just say 'the prison', and YLT's 'round-house' guesses at a derivation. The word is uncommon and its origin is argued: R. Abraham (Ibn Ezra, as reported by Ramban) took it as an Egyptian name which the text explains in the next phrase, 'the place where the king's prisoners are bound'; Ramban rejects that and thinks it an underground pit with a small opening above. This matters to the scene: it is a royal prison, for the king's prisoners, which is why the cupbearer and baker of the next chapter are put in with him (Gen 40:3 places it in the house of the captain of the guard). He is now in the world of the court.

The verse also plays on one root. 'The king's prisoners' and 'were bound' both come from אסר, 'to bind'; the second is a passive participle, the first a noun. Hear the repetition as a clang of chain. And note the last clause, which seems redundant: 'he was there, in the house of the Sohar.' The Hebrew repeats the place name to underline that he stays: Radak reads it to mean his master never changed his mind.

philological_notes.note: A Ketiv/Qere pair on word 11. The consonantal text is read with the passive participle form (asurei, written, Ketiv); the reading tradition says asirei (Qere), 'prisoners of'. Radak: the Ketiv is a passive form, the Qere an adjectival/noun form, and the sense is the same. Both belong to this one word; the second 'asurim' (word 13) is a separate verb form of the same root, 'were bound'.

'House of the Sohar', the prison. The word's origin is disputed. Ramban (reporting R. Abraham) mentions an Egyptian word explained by the text itself, then gives his own view of an underground pit, connected with a round shape or with Aramaic 'moon'. The KJV 'prison' is a fair sense; the specific word is not translated.
'Bound', passive participle of the same root as 'prisoners'. Together they produce the sound-play 'prisoners … bound'.

token_glosses.gloss: the prisoners of (written: the bound of)

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH was with Joseph, and extended to him steadfast kindness, and gave his favor in the eyes of the commander of the house of the Sohar.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD was with Joseph. In the dark, in the bonds, the LORD was with him, and bent his steadfast kindness toward him, and gave him favor in the eyes of the one who commanded the prison.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera cuts from the wife's noise to a quiet sentence that opens with the word 'And', not 'But': the Hebrew does not argue against the prison, it simply states, again, what has been true since 39:2 and 39:3: YHWH was with Joseph. Nothing in the verse lifts him out; what changes is how he is seen.

Two words carry it. Chesed is the loyal, faithful kindness one owes a bond; the Hebrew has God 'extend' (nata, 'stretch out', as a hand is stretched) it to Joseph. The KJV's 'shewed him mercy' suggests a pardon, which does not come, and misses the loyalty in the word. Rashi hears something else in chesed: that Joseph was found pleasing by all who saw him, with the Mishnah's phrase for a bride, 'beautiful and gracious'. The second word, chen, 'favor', is what God 'gives' in the eyes of the sar, the commander, which is a rank, not a 'keeper'; the KJV's 'keeper of the prison' makes him a turnkey. He is an official, and Joseph will be placed under him.

The pattern is deliberate: in verse 2 God was with him in Potiphar's house, and here he is again in a prison. The location changes; the structure of the story does not.

philological_notes.note: Steadfast, loyal kindness, the goodwill that keeps faith with a relationship. Here God 'extends' it. Rashi reads it differently, as charm: Joseph was acceptable to all who saw him, comparing the Mishnah's description of a bride as 'beautiful and gracious'.
'His favor', the gracious regard he finds with another. God 'gives' it in the eyes of the commander; compare Gen 39:4, where Joseph found favor in Potiphar's eyes.
'Commander of the house of the Sohar'. Sar is an officer's title (compare 'commander of the guard'), not a gaoler's. The KJV's 'keeper' flattens it.

verses.translation_literal: And the commander of the house of the prison gave into the hand of Joseph all the prisoners who were in the house of the prison, and all that they were doing there, he was the doer.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the prison's commander put all the prisoners into Joseph's hand, every one of them. And whatever was done there, it was Joseph who did it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reversal is stunning in its economy. The man who entered as a convict now holds the keys. The Hebrew has the same phrase that marked his rise in Potiphar's house: 'into his hand' (39:4-6). Repetition tells the audience that the pattern has returned: wherever Joseph is, what is entrusted to him prospers.

The last clause, 'he was the doer', is a stiff phrase that the KJV and Webster render in several ways. Ibn Ezra and Radak (following Onkelos) read it as 'nothing was done there except on his word, as though he himself did it'. A prisoner is made an administrator.

philological_notes.note: 'He was the doer': a periphrastic participle that stresses continuing action. Radak, following the Targum, takes it as 'nothing was done except on his word'.

verses.translation_literal: There was no commander of the house of the Sohar seeing any thing at all in his hand, because YHWH [was] with him; and that which he was doing, YHWH was making succeed.
verses.translation_dramatic: The commander of the prison did not look at anything in Joseph's hand, not a thing, for the LORD was with him. And whatever Joseph's hands did, the LORD made it come out right.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse closes the chapter's refrain. The commander 'does not see' anything in Joseph's hand: Radak notes that 'any thing at all' (kol me'umah) stresses how little he looked. The KJV's 'looked not to' is archaic English for 'did not check on'. To play it: a man who has stopped counting.

The reason is given in two clauses, and YHWH is named in both, as the subject each time: 'because YHWH was with him', and, with Joseph's work put first for emphasis, 'that which he was doing, YHWH was making succeed'. The verbs are participles, which render an ongoing action: this was the steady state of the place, not a single event. Joseph does, YHWH makes succeed; the chapter gives the credit to God twice in one breath. Rashi simply glosses 'because YHWH was with him' as 'for the sake of that'. The Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds that the commander had no need to guard Joseph as he did the other prisoners.

Note also the echo of 'hand' (yad): in 39:4-6 Potiphar placed everything 'in his hand', and here the commander sees nothing 'in his hand'. The prison becomes a second Potiphar's house, with Joseph again running it from below.

philological_notes.note: 'Anything at all': Radak reads kol as stressing how little the commander examined; the word is mostly found in negatives.
'Making succeed', a Hiphil participle with YHWH as subject: the success is done to Joseph's work by God. The participle gives it a continuing sense, 'was making succeed'.

events.title: Potiphar buys Joseph from the Ishmaelites
events.narrative_summary: Joseph is brought down to Egypt, where Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, buys him from the Ishmaelites.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Verse 1 resumes the sale of Gen 37:36 after the Judah interlude, so it is the same moment: anchored on the START of evt.gen_37.sold_to_potiphar, 1 hour, margin 1 day.

events.title: The LORD is with Joseph and he prospers in Potiphar's house
events.narrative_summary: The LORD is with Joseph and he prospers in the house of his Egyptian master. His master sees that the LORD makes all he does succeed.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word. Half a year after the purchase for him to settle (offset 6 months), then about a year of visible success (margin 6 months); MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Potiphar makes Joseph overseer of all he owns
events.narrative_summary: Joseph finds favour, serves Potiphar and is set over the house and everything Potiphar has. The LORD blesses the house for his sake, and Potiphar knows nothing but the food he eats. Joseph is handsome in form and appearance.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'From the time he appointed him' (v5) starts the blessed period. No length is given; I took 3 years of stewardship, starting at the end of the prospering (margin 6 months). Rashbam on v6: Potiphar saw the household only at meals. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Potiphar's wife looks at Joseph and says, 'Lie with me'
events.narrative_summary: After these things Potiphar's wife lifts her eyes to Joseph and says, 'Lie with me.'
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'After these things' (v7) with no interval: one year after the end of the stewardship period, margin a year. MACRO_ERA.

events.title: Joseph refuses: how could he sin against God?
events.narrative_summary: Joseph refuses and tells her that his master has withheld nothing from him but her, and that he cannot do this great evil and sin against God.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A reply in the same exchange, about 5 minutes. It takes the tier of the scene's framing (MACRO_ERA).

events.title: She presses him day by day and he will not listen
events.narrative_summary: She speaks to Joseph day after day, and he does not listen to her, to lie with her or to be with her.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Day by day' (v10) is repeated daily speech; the length is not given. About 2 months, margin 1 month; Ibn Ezra on v11 would allow a week, a month or a year.

events.title: Joseph enters the empty house and flees, leaving his garment
events.narrative_summary: One day Joseph goes into the house to do his work, with none of the household there. She seizes him by his garment, and he leaves it in her hand, flees and goes out.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'About this day' (v11) follows the pressure of v10; no hour is given. Rashi: a festival; Radak: one of those days of her insistence. Duration 10 minutes, margin 1 month because the interval after v10 is open. DAY_SEQUENCE for the day it belongs to.

events.title: She calls the household and says the Hebrew came to mock them
events.narrative_summary: Seeing the garment in her hand and Joseph fled, she calls the men of her house and says that the Hebrew was brought to mock them, that he came to lie with her and that she cried out, so he left his garment and fled.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Straight after he flees (v13). 10 minutes; margin 1 hour.

events.title: She shows the garment to Potiphar and accuses Joseph
events.narrative_summary: She keeps his garment by her until her husband comes home, then repeats her story to him: the Hebrew servant he brought came to mock her, and fled leaving his garment when she cried out.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Until his lord came home' (v16) is a wait of hours the text does not fix; 6 hours after the cry, margin 4 hours. Same day, DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: Potiphar's anger burns and he puts Joseph in prison
events.narrative_summary: Potiphar's anger burns when he hears his wife's words, and he takes Joseph and puts him in the prison where the king's prisoners are kept.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the accusation at once (v19-20): 2 hours, margin a day. DAY_SEQUENCE.

events.title: The LORD is with Joseph in prison and the keeper trusts him
events.narrative_summary: The LORD shows Joseph steadfast love and gives him favour with the keeper of the prison, who puts all the prisoners and all that is done there in Joseph's hand and looks after nothing under his care.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No interval is given. A year before the keeper's trust is complete (offset 1 year), then two years in which it holds (margin 1 year). The stay is left open for Gen 40. MACRO_ERA.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Seeing the garment in her hand and Joseph fled, she calls the household with her version (v13-14).
In the prison where he was put, the LORD is with Joseph and gives him favour with the keeper (v20-21).
Potiphar sees that the LORD is with Joseph and prospers all he does, and so he sets him over his house (v3-4).
Her accusation answers Joseph's refusal, which left her spurned and his garment in her hand (v8-18).
Hearing his wife's words, Potiphar's anger burns and he imprisons Joseph (v19-20).

entities.summary_bio: The garment Joseph leaves in the wife's hand as he flees. She keeps it beside her as false evidence for her husband.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'ʿibrî', of uncertain origin, often linked to Eber or to 'crossing over'; used in the text by foreigners and for outsiders.
entities.summary_bio: The people descended from Eber, here used by Potiphar's wife as a label of contempt for Joseph, the foreign slave.
The other servants of Potiphar's house. None is inside when Joseph flees, so the wife's account to them rests on her word alone.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'ʾăsîrê hammelek', 'those bound by the king'.
entities.summary_bio: The men held in the prison under Pharaoh's authority. Joseph is placed among them and later put in charge of them.

aliases: the house of his master the Egyptian
entities.summary_bio: The household of Potiphar, captain of the guard, in Egypt. Joseph serves here, rises to run it, and is falsely accused here.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'bêt hassōhar'; 'sōhar' is probably 'round' or 'enclosure', though this is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The place where the king's prisoners are bound. Joseph is put here and, under the LORD's favour, comes to manage it.

aliases: commander of the house of the prison
entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew 'śar', commander or chief, of the 'bêt hassōhar', the round house or prison; the meaning of 'sōhar' is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The chief officer of the prison where the king's prisoners are held. Moved by the LORD's favour on Joseph, he puts all the prisoners and their work in Joseph's hand.

entities.etymology_meaning: Unnamed; the text calls her 'the wife of his master'.
entities.summary_bio: The wife of Potiphar, Joseph's master. She presses Joseph to lie with her, and when he flees she uses his garment to accuse him of assault, which sends him to prison.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 39:12 has it left in her hand and 39:16 says she laid it by her until her husband came home.
Gen 39:2 and 39:21 say the LORD was with Joseph, in the house and in the prison.
Gen 39:4 says Potiphar appointed him over his house and gave him all he had.
Gen 39:22 says the keeper put all the prisoners in Joseph's hand.
Gen 39:2 says he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
Gen 39:20 says Potiphar put him in the prison and he was there.
Gen 39:19 says his anger burned when he heard his wife's words.

systems.name: The LORD makes someone prosper
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East success was read as a sign of divine favour, and a patron deity's presence with a person was shown by outcomes. Genesis presents Israel's God as the source of prosperity even in foreign households and for non-Israelites near the chosen one.
rules_and_mechanics: The LORD is 'with' a person and makes what they do succeed.
Blessing can extend to the household of the one favoured (Gen 39:5).

systems.name: False accusation
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Laws in the region required witnesses and punished false witness, but a household head could act on the word of a spouse. A slave accused of sexual offence against the master's wife had little protection.
rules_and_mechanics: An accuser calls others by outcry and tells the story first.
Physical evidence (a garment) is offered in place of witnesses.
The accused slave is not recorded as answering.

systems.name: Imprisonment
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Egypt held state prisoners in royal prisons run by officers; imprisonment was mostly detention before further decision rather than a fixed sentence.
rules_and_mechanics: A master or official puts the person into custody.
The prison is a place for the king's prisoners, bound under a keeper.
No trial or term is recorded.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The wife calls the household and says the Hebrew came to mock them and she cried out.
system_instances.significance_note: She casts Joseph as a foreigner and gets the household on her side before her husband returns.

system_instances.outcome_summary: She repeats the charge to Potiphar, with the garment beside her, and blames him for bringing the Hebrew in.
system_instances.significance_note: The garment, the evidence of his innocence, becomes proof against him.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD blesses Potiphar's house and fields for Joseph's sake.
system_instances.significance_note: It shows blessing flowing to outsiders through Joseph, as promised to Abraham's line.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Potiphar, angry, puts Joseph in the prison for the king's prisoners.
system_instances.significance_note: It is Joseph's second descent, and the way he will meet Pharaoh's officials.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD is with Joseph and all he does succeeds, which Potiphar sees.
system_instances.significance_note: It explains why a slave is trusted and sets the contrast with his later fall.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD shows him loyalty and favour, and the keeper leaves everything to him.
system_instances.significance_note: The pattern of 39:2-6 repeats in prison, showing God's presence did not leave him.

edges.description: Joseph refuses, citing his master's trust and sin against God.
The keeper puts all the prisoners and their work in Joseph's hand.
Potiphar appoints Joseph over his house and puts all he owns in his hand.
Potiphar buys Joseph from the Ishmaelites.
Potiphar takes Joseph and puts him in the prison.
She tells the household the Hebrew came in to mock them and to lie with her.
She tells Potiphar the Hebrew servant came in to mock her.
She catches Joseph by his garment and repeats her demand.
Potiphar's wife looks at Joseph and tells him to lie with her.
The LORD blesses Potiphar's house for Joseph's sake.
The LORD extends steadfast love to Joseph and gives him favour with the keeper.
The LORD makes everything Joseph does succeed.
